items.full: From July through September 2026, the WordPress Community organized 39 events with the financial support of the project’s five Global Partners : Jetpack, WordPress.com, WooCommerce, Bluehost, and Hostinger. From a small gathering of 56 in Mannheim to a Contributor Day in the Philippines that drew 322 people, and the first-ever WordCamp in Eket, Nigeria, these events brought newcomers, contributors, and builders together around the world. The 39 events were too many to cover in one post, so this recap highlights a few of the moments that stood out. The quarter opened in July with WordCamp Mannheim , a small event with real range. The 56 attendees covered topics from AI and WordPress block development to current security know-how, along with presentations on values, training, and the open web. In August, the momentum moved to Nigeria, where Eket held its inaugural WordCamp on August 15 under the theme “From Idea to Income: Building Opportunities with WordPress.” Engr. Aniebiet Udoh took the stage for the keynote, challenging attendees to embrace the global reach of the web: “The internet has no small towns.” He urged creators to follow a five-step path: Later in August, WordCamp Philippines drew approximately 434 attendees, contributors and first-time attendees, to Iloilo City on August 28-29. One of the highlights of Contributor Day was the Open Source Library, an activity inspired by the Human Library concept. Instead of borrowing a book, participants could “borrow” a person and spend time having a meaningful conversation about their experiences, careers, communities, and journeys in open source. WordPress.com ran both a booth and a dedicated Community + Education table. The education table alone generated connections with 14 schools and universities, sparked three new meetup applications, and produced a new Campus Connect application from Colegio San Agustin in Bacolod. In Uganda, WordPress is reaching people who have never worked with it before. The third edition of WordCamp Masaka welcomed students and first-timers to participate in a hands-on WordPress Practical session. Led by community members, Stephen Dumba and Cinderella Mbabazi, Florence Namyalo , the Founder and CEO of RAPCIO, and the IT team of Equator University of Science and Technology, the group installed WordPress, explored the dashboard, and began building websites. In September, nearly half of this year’s participants at WordCamp Jinja were students. One of them, fascinated by the WordPress ecosystem and its spirit of generosity and inclusivity, drew all the sponsor logos by hand so he could remember them after the event. In September, WordCamp Costa Rica brought together 327 people. A noteworthy highlight was the pre-event WordPress Studio workshop, where 25 participants each built and launched a live site on WordPress.com in a single morning. The event also demonstrated the growing pipeline from education to community. At least 100 attendees came to WordCamp Costa Rica after first experiencing WordPress through WordPress Campus Connect events at Beenova and UCR Esparza earlier in the year. items.desc: Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web , a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites. The book draws … Andy Clarke answers six questions about Standout Designs for the Web originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. Web designer, author, and Stuff & Nonsense founder Andy Clarke has released Standout Designs for the Web , a new e-book that encourages designers to move beyond familiar templates and conventional layouts to create more personality-driven websites. The book draws on Clarke’s thirty years of web design experience. It explores how storytelling, color, typography, imagery, and layout can work together to create websites that people recognize and remember. We asked Andy a few questions about the book and the ideas that went into it. Question: What made you want to write this book? I’ve been designing websites for over thirty years, and I can’t remember a time when designers had more tools, techniques, and technology available to them. Yet, somehow, so many websites look remarkably similar. I’m not suggesting every website needs a novelty design. Far from it. But I do think that — somewhere along the way—designers have become a little too comfortable with familiar patterns and predictable layouts. I wrote Standout Designs for the Web to encourage designers to rediscover the creativity and personality that made me fall in love with the web in the first place. Question: What’s wrong with websites looking similar? Isn’t familiarity a good thing? Absolutely. Familiarity helps people understand how websites work, and there’s no reason to make something difficult to use just to be different. The problem is when familiarity makes every design look alike. When you visit a hotel website, an insurance company, or an online shop, you should be able to recognise something of the company behind it. I call this sameness “commodity design,” and it’s perfectly fine when all you want is fine, but it does little to make a company recognisable or its website memorable. I’m not arguing against using conventions. I’m asking designers to make more thoughtful decisions about when to use them. Question: You talk a lot about storytelling. What does that actually mean for web design? When I talk about storytelling, I don’t mean writing a lengthy company history or filling a website with marketing messages. Every company has a story worth telling. It might be how it started, the people behind it, its personality, or something unexpected about what it does. Those details can influence everything from the words you write to the colours, typography, illustrations, and layouts you choose. I spend a lot of time talking to clients because I’m looking for what makes them different. Sometimes, something they mention almost in passing becomes the inspiration for an entire design. The trick is recognising which details are worth developing and turning them into something visual. Question: Why did you invent a fake company for getaway drivers to demonstrate your ideas? Ha! Because I wanted a vehicle for my explanations and to have some fun. Wheelman is a fictional company for getaway drivers, and it gave me the freedom to explore ideas without worrying too much about the practical constraints of a real client project. items.desc: Contributors to the Costa Rican Spanish locale are making WordPress more accessible to Spanish-speaking communities in Costa Rica. Students from local schools and universities have joined the Polyglots team, helping translate WordPress.org projects and review community contributions. Students from two universities and a bilingual high school in Costa Rica contributed through the WordPress Credits program, […]
items.full: Contributors to the Costa Rican Spanish locale are making WordPress more accessible to Spanish-speaking communities in Costa Rica. Students from local schools and universities have joined the Polyglots team, helping translate WordPress.org projects and review community contributions. Students from two universities and a bilingual high school in Costa Rica contributed through the WordPress Credits program , which lets students earn academic credit for contributing to WordPress as part of their studies. On the Polyglots team, contributors suggest translations for WordPress Core, plugins, themes, and WordPress.org sites. Locale editors review and approve those suggestions. Between September 2025 and November 2026, translation coverage in es_CR rose from 38% to 100% on WordPress.org, from 39% to 98% in the Plugin Directory, and from 45% to 99% in the Forums. WordPress Core reached 99%, while the queue of strings waiting for review fell from 665 to 105. One participating school, Liceo Experimental Bilingüe José Figueres Ferrer in Cartago, was the first high school in the Americas to implement WordPress Credits through its Student Community Service program, Trabajo Comunal Estudiantil. Its students focused on Polyglots and helped advance the es_CR translations. WP Credits pushed me to contribute to something real, not just a class assignment. Going from not knowing what a ‘string’ was to translating hundreds of them was a great feeling, and it showed me that even a ‘small’ contribution like translation genuinely helps people who use WordPress in Spanish every day. The project also produced a resource for new contributors. The video “ Cómo contribuir en el equipo de traducción ” walks viewers through contributing on the WordPress translation platform, using Costa Rican Spanish as an example. If you read and write a language other than English, you can help make WordPress more useful to people in your language. Start with the first steps in the Polyglots Handbook to learn how to suggest translations and take part in the review process. Then check the translation stats page to find projects that need work in your locale. Educators can explore the WordPress Credits program to learn how students can contribute to WordPress as part of their studies.

items.title: OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
items.desc: OpenAI has significantly strengthened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In adaptive red-teaming tests, the success rate for extracting protected reasoning fell from 54 percent to 0.2 percent. The company is also suspending thousands to tens of thousands of accounts each week over coordinated distillation campaigns. The article OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says . The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too. The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems combine targeted training, input and output filters for messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly. Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red teaming against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower is better. Ad Anthropic is fighting systematic distillation attacks as well , also banning tens of thousands of accounts to curb the theft of internal reasoning, reportedly succeeding in 90 to 99 percent of cases. The article Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat" to privacy. OS-level AI like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture screen content to complete user tasks. That undermines end-to-end encryption by letting agents pull decrypted messages straight from the display and process them externally. Meta's AI agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions, including accessibility tools and screenshots on macOS. Meta says this happened only with explicit user permission. Ad Signal already blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but calls its defenses incomplete: macOS screenshots can't be reliably blocked, and AI access to file systems and notifications remains a risk. Signal says Apple, Google, and Microsoft should make it easy to block AI agents from apps entirely. Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.full: 20th November 2026 - Link Blog Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) . Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. This is a link post by Simon Willison, posted on 20th November 2026 . items.title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
items.desc: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous open problem for 167 years, with a proof formalized in Lean that spans over 250,000 pages. Just hours later, Stanford researchers published an independent, entirely human competing proof, and mathematicians are now checking whether either one holds up. The article Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem. Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement . According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well. Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line. To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line. Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says. Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo. "It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said. Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away. About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote. Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them.
